concepts.name: Hedging for tail latency, and its side-effect risk
The Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern (202, status endpoint, 303)

choices.text: Nothing: `ComputeTotal` isn't called at all
`ComputeTotal` runs, then the assignment is skipped
It throws `NullReferenceException` on the assignment
It doesn't compile: `?.` can't be on the left of `=`

questions.explanation: C# 14 allows `?.` and `?[]` on the left of an assignment. The right-hand side is evaluated only when the left side is non-null, so the line is equivalent to `if (order is not null) order.Total = ComputeTotal();` and `ComputeTotal` never runs here. Before C# 14 the line didn't compile, which is why the last choice is tempting.

sources.title: What's new in C# 14
sources.claim: In C# 14 the null-conditional operators ?. and ?[] can be used on the left of an assignment or compound assignment; the right side is evaluated only when the left side isn't null, so `customer?.Order = GetCurrentOrder();` doesn't call GetCurrentOrder when customer is null.

questions.prompt: Calls to a read-only catalog API usually return in 50 ms, but some hang for seconds on one bad replica. Which resilience strategy is built to cut this tail by starting a parallel attempt when the first one is slow?

choices.text: Hedging: after a delay it starts another try and uses the first good result
Retry with jitter: it sends a new attempt the moment the first one gets slow
A circuit breaker: it sends each call to a healthy replica at the same time
A total timeout: it re-sends the request whenever an attempt runs too long

questions.explanation: Hedging (Polly's latency mode, or `AddStandardHedgingHandler` in .NET) starts an extra attempt once the first has taken longer than a delay (2 seconds by default), returns the first acceptable result and cancels the others. Retry waits for an attempt to fail before trying again, a circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency, and a timeout only cuts an attempt off.

sources.title: Hedging resilience strategy
sources.claim: In latency mode, hedging triggers additional executions when the initial ones take too long (Delay defaults to 2 seconds), and when an acceptable result arrives it cancels the pending actions before returning it.

sources.title: Build resilient HTTP apps: Key development patterns
sources.claim: The standard hedging handler retries slow requests in parallel; its pipeline is a total timeout, hedging, then per-endpoint rate limiter, circuit breaker and attempt timeout.

questions.prompt: `POST /reports` starts a report that takes 2 to 5 minutes, and clients time out waiting for the response. Design the HTTP contract using the Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern.

model_answer.summary: Accept the work at once with `202 Accepted` and a `Location` pointing at a status endpoint, let clients poll it, and redirect them to the result when the work is done; make the POST safe to retry.
key_points: Validate the request, queue the work and return `202 Accepted` immediately, with a `Location` header for a status endpoint and a `Retry-After` hint for how often to poll
While the work runs, the status endpoint returns `200 OK` with a status body (pending, running, failed); when it completes it returns `303 See Other` to the result resource, or the result itself
Accept an `Idempotency-Key` so a retried POST returns the existing operation instead of starting a second report
Where clients can take pushes (webhooks, SignalR or Server-Sent Events) those can replace polling; give status resources a retention period

questions.explanation: The pattern decouples a long job from the HTTP request that starts it: the client gets a fast acknowledgement and a URL to check, instead of holding a connection open for minutes. A `303` makes the client GET the result rather than replay the POST, which `302` doesn't guarantee. The idempotency key matters because a client can't tell a lost `202` from a request that never arrived.

sources.title: Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern
sources.claim: The API validates the request and returns HTTP 202 with Location and Retry-After headers; the status endpoint returns 200 with the current state while work runs and 303 See Other to the result when done; clients can supply an Idempotency-Key; the pattern may not suit cases where WebSockets/SignalR, Server-Sent Events or callbacks are available, and status resources need a retention policy.

questions.prompt: In C# 14, `cart` may be null. Which of these lines does **not** compile?

choices.text: `cart?.Count += 1;`
`cart?.Owner = customer;`
`cart?.Discount -= 5m;`
`cart?.Count++;`

questions.explanation: Null-conditional assignment allows plain assignment and every compound assignment (`+=`, `-=` and so on), each evaluated only when `cart` isn't null. Increment and decrement (`++`, `--`) are not allowed on a null-conditional expression, so write `cart?.Count += 1;` instead.

sources.title: Member access and null-conditional operators and expressions - C# reference
sources.claim: Beginning in C# 14, assignment is permissible with a null-conditional access expression; any form of compound assignment such as += or -= is allowed, but increment (++) and decrement (--) aren't.

questions.prompt: A teammate adds `AddStandardHedgingHandler()` to the `HttpClient` that sends `POST /payments` to a payment provider. What is the main risk?

choices.text: Hedging only supports GET, so the POST calls fail at startup
Parallel attempts may each reach the provider and charge twice
It has no circuit breaker, so a failing provider gets no relief
It has no total timeout, so a payment call can hang forever

questions.explanation: Hedging sends extra attempts in parallel while the first is still running. Cancelling the slower ones doesn't undo work the server already did, so a non-idempotent POST can be processed twice; Polly warns that hedged actions can run several times in parallel. The standard hedging handler does include a 30-second total timeout and a circuit breaker per endpoint, and nothing restricts it to GET.

sources.title: Build resilient HTTP apps: Key development patterns
sources.claim: Hedging retries slow requests in parallel; the standard hedging handler chains a 30-second total request timeout, hedging, and per-endpoint rate limiter, circuit breaker and attempt timeout.

sources.title: Hedging resilience strategy
sources.claim: The hedging strategy can spawn multiple parallel executions of the same action, so the action may run more than once.

questions.prompt: In the Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern, the status endpoint finds that the job is finished and its result is at `/reports/42`. What should it return?

choices.text: `302 Found` and `Location: /reports/42`, the usual redirect
`202 Accepted` again, with the finished report in the body
`303 See Other` and `Location: /reports/42` for a GET
`404 Not Found` on the status URL, so polling stops

questions.explanation: `303 See Other` tells the client to fetch the redirect URL with GET whatever the original method was, which is right because the client is retrieving a separate result. `302 Found` doesn't guarantee the method change, and some clients replay the original request, which can cause duplicate POSTs. `202` means the work was only accepted, and a `404` is ambiguous with an invalid request ID.

sources.title: Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern
sources.claim: If the status endpoint redirects after completion, use HTTP 303 See Other, which makes the client GET the redirect URL; 302 doesn't guarantee a method change and some clients replay the original method; polling the resource for 404 is unclear because invalid IDs also return 404.

questions.prompt: `POST /reports` starts a report that takes 2 to 5 minutes, and clients time out waiting. You adopt the Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern: which belong in the HTTP contract? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Return `202 Accepted` at once, with a `Location` header for a status endpoint
When the report is done, the status endpoint answers `303 See Other` to the result
Accept an `Idempotency-Key`, so a retried POST returns the existing operation
Hold the POST open until the report is ready, then return `201 Created`
When done, the status endpoint answers `302 Found`, which forces clients to GET

questions.explanation: The pattern acknowledges the work at once with `202 Accepted` and a `Location` (plus `Retry-After`) for a status endpoint the client polls. When the work completes, `303 See Other` sends the client to the result with a GET, whatever the original method was. An `Idempotency-Key` matters because a client can't tell a lost `202` from a request that never arrived, so a retry must not start a second report. Holding the POST open is the timeout problem the pattern removes, and `302 Found` doesn't guarantee a method change: some clients replay the POST.

sources.title: Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern
sources.claim: The API returns HTTP 202 with Location and Retry-After headers; when the work completes the status endpoint returns 303 See Other, which makes the client GET the result, while 302 Found doesn't guarantee a method change; clients can supply an Idempotency-Key so a duplicate POST returns the existing status resource.
